title: The hours only count once
author: Child Development Matters
summary: This piece takes on the parental hope that practising one demanding skill, such as piano or coding, will quietly lift the whole mind. It separates near transfer, which happens often enough, from far transfer, which almost never does. Drawing on meta-analyses of roughly seven thousand children in music studies, it shows that the small positive effect disappears once studies use active control groups and random assignment. The same pattern holds for video games and other brain-training activities, where the best predictor of a glowing result is a loosely run study. The author explains this through the idea that practice wears a groove into the specific pathways a task uses rather than tuning an all-purpose engine. The conclusion is that activities should be chosen for what they are, with any wider benefit treated as a gift, while remembering that group averages cannot rule out a particular child for whom the piano mattered.
points: Far transfer, where practising one skill lifts general thinking, is the hope behind many enrichment choices but almost never shows up in well-designed studies.
In music studies the apparent benefit falls to zero once researchers compare against another lively activity and assign children at random, at any age and for any length of lessons.
Identical-twin comparisons give a clean test: the twin who took up music does not end up with a higher IQ.
Practice improves the specific circuits a task uses rather than a shared mental engine, so the effort stays where it is spent.
Parents can value music, games and other pursuits for their own sake, since the case for them never depended on making children generally cleverer.
quotes: Near transfer is when practising something helps with very similar things, and it happens often enough. Far transfer is when practising one thing lifts the whole mind, so the piano makes the sums easier and the puzzles make the essays sharper.

In the ones that did the dull, essential things, comparing music against another lively activity rather than against nothing, and deciding at random which child got which, the effect slides down and sits at zero.
Among identical twins, the one who took up music does not end up with a higher IQ than the twin who did not. Same genes, different hobby, same task performance.
Music is worth a childhood on its own terms, for the pleasure of it, for the sound a house makes when someone in it is learning to play. It is simply not a side door into a bigger brain.
The effect on general thinking is minimal, and the thing that best predicts a glowing result is not how much cleverer anyone got, but how loosely the study was run.

Practice wears its groove into the exact pathways a task uses, and the improvement stays in that groove, a physical change in the circuits that task runs on rather than a tune-up of some all-purpose engine another task could borrow.

You get better at the thing you practise, a little better at its near neighbours, and that is mostly where it stops. So choose the music for the music, and the rest for whatever it truly gives your child.
